<reason>B wins the central comparison: A did not establish why recognition would reach protected perpetrators better than coordinated enforcement of specified environmental offenses. B distinguished jurisdiction from immunity, corrected A’s misrepresentation of its conditional domestic-law concession, and exposed inconsistent assurances about lawful projects. A’s complementary-tool argument and proportionality analogies had force, but its categorical claim that recognition closes the accountability gap remained unsupported.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B’s second rebuttal exposed the permit dilemma: if approval shields defendants, sponsoring states can authorize destruction; if it does not, A’s promised protection for assessed, mitigated, lawful projects disappears. A’s closing accepted that permits were merely evidence without resolving the underlying uncertainty over criminal liability.</best_rebuttal>
